terms.grammar: demonstrative pronoun and adjective; genitive illīus, dative illī
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.18.2: cētera bellē; illud mīror
terms.comment: What is away from both speaker and listener, in place or in time; with hic, “this … that”. The neuter often points ahead to what follows: illud mīror, “one thing surprises me”. After a name it marks someone famous (see “the”).

evidence: Mart. 4.49.10: laudant illa, sed ista legunt
terms.comment: The demonstrative of the person spoken to: what is near you or yours, or what you are talking about (Lewis & Short). Hence the adverbs istīc, istūc, istinc, there where you are.

evidence: Cic. Amic. 80: est enim is quī est tamquam alter īdem
Ter. Ad. 978: Ob eam rem? — Ob eam.
terms.comment: The weak “that”: it points back to what has been named, and stands before a relative: is quī, the one who; id quod, that which, what.

phrases.latin: phasēlus ille, quem vidētis, hospitēs, ait fuisse nāvium celerrimus
phrases.english: that boat you see, my guests, says she was once the fastest of ships

phrases.latin: cōnfiteor: laudant illa, sed ista legunt
phrases.english: I admit it: they praise those, but they read these

phrases.latin: ille terrārum mihi praeter omnīs angulus rīdet
phrases.english: that corner of the earth smiles on me above all others
everything else is fine; one thing surprises me

phrases.latin: quaesō … mihi, mī Catulle, paulum istōs commodā
phrases.english: please, my Catullus, lend me those men of yours for a little while

phrases.latin: est enim is quī est tamquam alter īdem
phrases.english: for a friend is one who is, as it were, a second self
